rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient while holding its window and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure the critical pair’s sensitivity to slope.
The six-minute gradient retains full resolution, with the closest pair at R=2.46. Test the next shorter grid duration to reduce analysis time while checking that this pair remains above R=1.5.

The four-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Raise temperature at fixed gradient to test whether altered selectivity permits a faster fully resolved separation.

Heating sharply reduced the first pair’s resolution, so test cooling at the same gradient to establish the opposite selectivity response. Any added resolution margin could support a shorter gradient or a higher starting organic fraction.
Cooling improved the critical pair to R=2.48. Test the minimum gradient duration at this temperature to determine whether that selectivity gain can preserve full resolution in a faster run.

Narrow the organic window to reduce gradient steepness and recover the first pair’s missing resolution at the minimum gradient duration. The higher starting fraction removes some early low-organic time, while the final hold should allow the last compound to elute promptly.

Shift the window upward while preserving the successful gradient slope to accelerate the last peak’s elution. Check whether the higher starting organic fraction preserves the first pair’s resolution, which currently has only a small margin above 1.5.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the run further while making the gradient slightly shallower. Monitor the first pair closely because its earlier elution may offset the resolution benefit of the reduced slope.

Raise temperature by one step to shorten late retention while using the first pair’s modest resolution margin. Keep the gradient fixed to determine whether R remains at least 1.5 despite the unfavorable temperature trend seen earlier.

Test one higher starting-organic step to shorten late elution and reduce gradient steepness. This probes the early-retention boundary: the first pair must remain resolved despite moving closer to the solvent front.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early retention and test the next temperature step. This brackets the temperature limit for the fastest fully resolved method found so far; injection 10 remains the fallback if the first pair drops below R=1.5.

Narrow the gradient to recover the first pair’s resolution at 35 C while retaining the minimum gradient duration. This tests whether reduced steepness offsets the temperature-induced selectivity loss without excessive late-peak retention during the hold.

Lower the starting fraction to retain the early pair longer and return to the temperature that preserved full resolution. The narrower window should provide more resolution margin than injection 10 while keeping the separation short.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 14 to accelerate the last peak while testing whether the first pair retains full resolution. This refines a maximum-CRF alternative with better early retention than injection 10.
Test a slightly shallower gradient adjacent to the fastest maximum-CRF method, injection 10. This may improve the critical pair’s resolution margin with only a small increase in late-peak retention.

Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method. Test a shallower gradient with a trimmed starting window for a short maximum-CRF alternative offering more resolution margin for the critical pair.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step from injection 17 to keep the early pair retained longer and test whether its resolution improves. This seeks a larger resolution margin in a short maximum-CRF method, while retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved option.

Combine the short gradient of injection 15 with the cooler temperature that improved early-pair selectivity. This should provide additional resolution margin in a roughly three-minute separation; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 19 to test a faster alternative with more resolution margin than the 30 C methods. Injection 9 suggests that this starting fraction still retains the first pair adequately at 25 C.

Cool the successful method from injection 18 to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while keeping all peaks well within ten minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a less marginal alternative to the fastest confirmed method, injection 10.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 19 to seek more critical-pair resolution while retaining the minimum gradient duration and adequate early retention. This should offer a short maximum-CRF alternative with greater resolution margin; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 22 to slightly shorten late retention while testing whether the shallower gradient adds critical-pair resolution margin. This refines the short, fully resolved region without repeating a method; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF option.

Raise temperature one step from injection 23 to shorten late retention while using its critical-pair resolution margin. This tests an intermediate temperature between the fully resolved 25 C result and the marginally unresolved 35 C result at the same gradient.

Test a lower starting fraction near the fastest fully resolved methods to improve early retention while retaining the strongest endpoint and minimum gradient duration. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method if this steeper gradient compromises the first pair.
